outline.description: Sets out the employment context, the 2019 overtime policy change, the claims and remedies Cohen sought, the parties’ stipulations and payments, and how the case reached the Eighth Circuit on summary judgment.
subtopics: Parties and roles: Consilio as a nationwide legal document review company; Cohen as an hourly licensed attorney document reviewer in Minnesota
2019 policy change: email announcing elimination of overtime premium pay and paying all hours at base rate
Claims and statutes invoked: MPWA (§§ 181.101, 181.171), MFLSA (§§ 177.25, 177.27, subd. 8), MWTA (§ 181.032(d)(4), (f)); remedies sought (overtime, liquidated damages, penalties, injunctive relief)

Consilio’s payments and stipulations: $256,010.01 total to Minnesota reviewers; Cohen received $3,225.21 overtime and $462 liquidated damages; stipulation that all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages were paid; dispute remained over penalties
Procedural agreement: parties asked the district court to decide Consilio’s summary judgment motion first; district court granted summary judgment on all claims
Appellate standard of review and summary-judgment standard: de novo review; no genuine dispute of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law

outline.chapter_title: MPWA Penalties: Statutory Structure Limits Penalties to the Commissioner
outline.description: Explains why the court held that average daily wage penalties under § 181.101 are enforceable only by the Commissioner, not by private employees, and affirms summary judgment on this claim.
subtopics: Private right under § 181.171: civil action for violations of listed MPWA sections; recovery of compensatory damages and relief; civil penalties only if provided in the specific section violated
Text of § 181.101(a): penalties referenced solely in connection with the Commissioner’s demand-and-collection authority; money collected by the Commissioner must be paid to the employee
Employee’s preserved right under § 181.101(a): to prosecute a claim for wages (not penalties)

Textual-canons and comparators: legislative choice to expressly authorize employee penalties in §§ 181.13 and 181.14 shows it ‘knows how’ to do so (Lagasse; Hubbard); plain-language approach (Allan); supportive reading in Milner and Hull
Holding and disposition: only the Commissioner may seek average daily wage penalties under § 181.101; affirm summary judgment against Cohen’s MPWA penalty claim

outline.chapter_title: MFLSA Penalties: Standing, Mootness, and Voluntary Cessation Drive a Remand
outline.description: Analyzes the jurisdictional problem once wages and liquidated damages were paid and only civil penalties (payable to the Commissioner) remained, and why the Eighth Circuit vacated and remanded for a standing/mootness determination.
subtopics: What remains of the MFLSA claim: overtime wages and liquidated damages paid by stipulation; only statutory penalties sought—and both parties agree penalties are payable to the Commissioner
Article III requirements: plaintiff must have standing for each claim and form of relief (Town of Chester); standing must persist through the case (Sisney)
Civil penalties as redress: Laidlaw’s deterrence rationale; penalties can redress ongoing or threatened injury by deterring future violations

Voluntary cessation and mootness: case is moot only if it is absolutely clear the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur; unresolved fact question whether Consilio’s overtime policy remains in effect
Disposition on MFLSA: vacate summary judgment and remand for the district court to determine jurisdiction (standing/mootness) based on the policy’s current status and likelihood of recurrence

Special concurrence: Judge Kobes questions whether Laidlaw’s penalty rationale fits MFLSA’s scheme; suggests the district court may address mootness first; notes vacatur of fees, costs, and prejudgment interest in his view

outline.chapter_title: MWTA Notice Claim: No Identified Penalty Authority and Appellate Waiver
outline.description: Covers Cohen’s claim that Consilio failed to provide required notice of the policy change under the MWTA, why it failed on appeal, and the court’s reliance on waiver principles.
subtopics: MWTA theory: alleged failure to provide statutorily required written notice of change to overtime policy (§ 181.032(d)(4), (f))
Remedial gap: Cohen stipulated he received all pay owed; he identified no statutory authority for private civil penalties under the MWTA provisions invoked
Appellate briefing deficiency: lack of meaningful argument or legal authority constitutes waiver (Milligan)
Holding and disposition: affirm dismissal of the MWTA notice-based claim seeking penalties

outline.chapter_title: Injunctive Relief: Preserving Theories and the Limits of Summary-Judgment Briefing
outline.description: Explains why the court declined to consider Cohen’s revised request for injunctive relief raised at summary judgment rather than through the pleadings.
subtopics: Shift in requested relief: complaint sought specific injunctive remedies; summary-judgment briefing pivoted to an order rescinding the 2019 policy
Procedural rule: new claims or materially different relief must be raised by amending the complaint, not through opposition or summary-judgment briefs (InfoDeli; Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a))
Appellate posture: district court properly did not consider the new request; issue not preserved and not reviewed on appeal

Overall disposition and takeaways: court vacates and remands MFLSA penalties for jurisdictional determination; otherwise affirms (MPWA penalties, MWTA claim, and denial of belated injunctive relief); practice pointer to plead forward-looking relief early and maintain a live controversy
